title: Turning Savings into Income
description: A first-year withdrawal, the order of accounts, and the age-73 rule.
wolfLine: The 4% sketch is a choice. Age 73 is the requirement.

required-minimum-distribution.definition: The minimum you must withdraw from a traditional IRA and most workplace retirement plans. For an owner, it currently starts at age 73. A Roth IRA owner does not have this requirement during their lifetime.
required-minimum-distribution.example: Turn 73 this year and the traditional IRA starts a required withdrawal. The Roth IRA does not.

sequence-of-returns-risk.definition: The danger that bad returns arrive early in retirement, while you are withdrawing. The same average return is harsher if the bad years come first.
sequence-of-returns-risk.example: A 20% drop and then a $20,000 withdrawal leaves less than withdrawing from a pile that had not fallen.

annuity.definition: A contract with an insurance company. You pay a lump sum, and it pays you an income. The pile is often no longer yours to leave to someone else. This is a description, not a recommendation.
annuity.example: Handing over $100,000 for a lifetime income, and giving up that $100,000 as a pile.

lessons.title: The Withdrawal
lessons.summary: Four percent, once, then inflate the dollars.

steps.title: Year one
steps.body: The [[4% rule|four-percent-rule]] in year one is 4% of the portfolio. On $1,000,000 that is $40,000. Next year you adjust those dollars for inflation. You do not have to spend it all. Taking less is allowed. This is a sketch, and it is not the same thing as a required minimum distribution.

doc.title: Year one of a $1,000,000 pile
doc.subtitle: A rule of thumb, not a required minimum
doc.note: Later years adjust the $40,000 for inflation. They do not restart 4% on a new balance.

steps.prompt: How many dollars is the year-one withdrawal on this page?
Example inflation is 2%. What is the year-two withdrawal if you adjust the $40,000?
You must spend the whole $40,000.
steps.explain: It is a ceiling people use for planning. Spending less leaves more in the pile.

steps.prompt: What does year two adjust?
choices: The percent, restarted on whatever is left
steps.explain: Inflate the dollars. Do not recompute 4% of a shrunken balance and call it the same rule.

lessons.title: Which Account First
lessons.summary: A common order, not the only one.

steps.title: Taxable, then traditional, Roth last
steps.body: A common draw order: spend taxable brokerage money first, then [[traditional IRA|traditional-ira]] money, and leave the [[Roth IRA|roth-ira]] last. Roth withdrawals that are qualified are tax-free, and the owner has no required distribution. Traditional withdrawals are taxed. This is a common order. A tax pro can have a reason to swap it. It is not a command.

steps.prompt: Put the common draw order in order, Roth last.
items: Leave the Roth IRA for last
steps.explain: Taxable first, traditional in the middle, Roth last so the tax-free pile can keep growing.

steps.prompt: The common order empties the Roth IRA first.
steps.explain: Roth is last in this common order, not first.

steps.prompt: Why do people often save the Roth for last?
choices: Qualified withdrawals are tax-free, and the owner is not forced to take them
Because a Roth cannot hold a fund
steps.explain: Tax-free and no owner RMD. Traditional withdrawals are the taxable ones.

steps.prompt: In this common order, the account you spend first is the ___ brokerage.
steps.explain: Taxable. Roth waits.

steps.title: The age, for now
steps.body: A [[required minimum distribution]] is the least you must take from a traditional IRA and from most workplace plans. The starting age is 73. The first one can wait until April 1 of the next year, which can put two withdrawals in that next tax year. A Roth IRA owner does not have this requirement during their lifetime. The dollar amount uses an IRS table. This lesson grades the age, not a homemade table.

steps.prompt: At what age do traditional IRA required minimums currently start?
steps.explain: Age 73. The first withdrawal can be delayed until April 1 of the following year.

steps.prompt: A Roth IRA owner must start required minimums at 73.
steps.explain: Not during the owner’s lifetime. The traditional IRA is the one with the age-73 rule.

steps.prompt: Why might you take the first required withdrawal in the year you turn 73, instead of waiting until April 1?
choices: So you do not have two taxable withdrawals in the next year
steps.explain: Waiting until April 1 can stack two withdrawals into one tax year. Taking the first one in the year you turn 73 spreads them.

steps.prompt: You are allowed to withdraw more than the minimum.
steps.explain: The minimum is a floor. More is allowed, and it is taxable if it comes from a traditional account.

lessons.title: Bad Years First
lessons.summary: The order of returns matters once you are spending.

steps.title: Same average, harsher path
steps.body: [[Sequence-of-returns risk]] is what happens when the bad year comes while you are withdrawing. A $500,000 pile falls 20%, to $400,000, and you still take out $20,000. You have $380,000. If the pile had not fallen, the same withdrawal would leave $480,000. The early drop and the withdrawal stack.

steps.prompt: A $500,000 portfolio falls 20%. How many dollars is it worth before the withdrawal?
You then withdraw $20,000. How many dollars are left?
Without the drop, the same $20,000 withdrawal from $500,000 leaves how many dollars?
The order of returns stops mattering after you retire, because you are no longer contributing.
steps.explain: It matters more. Withdrawals turn an early drop into a smaller pile that then has to recover.

lessons.title: Annuities, Lightly
lessons.summary: Income in exchange for the pile.

steps.title: What you give up
steps.body: An [[annuity]] here means you pay an insurer a lump sum and it pays you an income, sometimes for life. The $100,000 is often no longer a pile you can leave to a child. Fees and the insurer’s promise are the whole product. This is a definition, not a suggestion to buy one.

docs.title: Keep the portfolio
docs.subtitle: You withdraw from it over time

docs.title: Hand it to an insurer
docs.subtitle: The pile is no longer yours to leave
docs.note: Income in exchange for the lump sum. Not a recommendation.

steps.prompt: Which page still leaves the $100,000 in your name?
steps.explain: The portfolio page is still yours. The annuity page traded the pile for an income stream.

steps.prompt: Buying an annuity is required once you retire.
steps.explain: It is one product. The withdrawal sketch does not require it.

steps.prompt: What is the usual trade?
choices: You give up the pile and receive an income
You keep the pile and the insurer also sends a gift
steps.explain: Income, in exchange for the lump sum. Read the fees before you ever think about it.

doc.title: Hand it to an insurer
doc.subtitle: The pile is no longer yours to leave
doc.note: Income in exchange for the lump sum. Not a recommendation.

steps.prompt: How many dollars leave your name on the annuity page?
steps.explain: The $100,000 is what you paid. It is not still a pile you control.

steps.title: Floors, then the rest
steps.body: The year-one sketch is $40,000. Housing needs at least $15,000, food at least $8,000, health at least $6,000, and everything else at least $1,000. Assign every dollar. The floors are the lesson. A real budget uses your bills.

steps.prompt: Assign all $40,000. Meet each floor.
steps.explain: The floors are $15,000, $8,000, $6,000, and $1,000, which add to $30,000. The other $10,000 can sit in everything else. That fill ends with $11,000 there.

steps.prompt: How many dollars do the four floors add up to, before the extra $10,000?
The $40,000 assignment is a bill from the IRS.
steps.explain: It is a spending sketch. The required minimum, if you are 73, is a different rule and a different math.

steps.prompt: What should a real version of this page use?
steps.explain: Your rent, your food, your premiums. The round numbers are only a drill.

lessons.title: The Check and the Pile
lessons.summary: Do not withdraw spending that Social Security already covers.

steps.title: Add them
steps.body: If Social Security pays $18,000 and spending is $50,000, the portfolio’s job is the $32,000 gap, not the whole $50,000. Withdrawing $50,000 anyway spends the pile faster than the plan. This is the same idea as a base and a gap, with a new set of numbers.

steps.prompt: Spending is $50,000 and Social Security is $18,000. How many dollars does the portfolio need to cover?
You withdraw the whole $50,000 anyway. How many extra dollars did you take beyond the gap?
steps.explain: $50,000 − $32,000 = $18,000. That extra is the Social Security you could have spent instead.

steps.prompt: Social Security and the portfolio withdrawal should both be large enough to cover all the spending, on purpose.
steps.explain: They stack. Covering the spending twice drains the portfolio.

steps.prompt: What is the portfolio’s job in this sketch?
choices: A second copy of all the spending
steps.explain: The gap. $32,000 here, not $50,000.

lessons.title: Joe and Ann’s First Year
lessons.summary: They are 66. The required minimum is not here yet.

story.title: The first retired year
story.character: Joe and Ann, both 66, newly retired
story.body:
Joe and Ann have a **$1,000,000** portfolio. A 4% year-one sketch is **$40,000**. They are **66**, so a required minimum has not started.

They spend taxable money first and leave the Roth IRA alone.

steps.title: Meet Joe and Ann
steps.body:
Joe and Ann are both 66 and newly retired. Their portfolio is $1,000,000. A 4% year-one sketch is $40,000. They are not 73, so a required minimum does not apply yet. The $40,000 is a choice.

They will spend taxable money first and leave the Roth IRA alone. They also write down what a 20% drop in year one would do, so the first bad year does not surprise them into selling everything.

steps.prompt: What is their year-one 4% withdrawal, in dollars?
Because they retired, they must take a required minimum at 66.
steps.explain: The traditional required minimum starts at 73. Sixty-six is a choice, not that rule.

steps.prompt: Which account do they spend first in the common order?
choices: A new annuity, required by law
steps.explain: Taxable first. The Roth waits. An annuity is not required.

steps.prompt: If the $1,000,000 fell 20% before any withdrawal, how many dollars would it be worth?
steps.explain: $1,000,000 × 0.80 = $800,000. That is the sequence risk they wrote down, not a prediction.

lessons.title: Sharpen Up
lessons.summary: Smart repetition on what you’re closest to forgetting.

lessons.title: Den Trial: Turning Savings into Income
lessons.summary: 8 questions. Three strikes and you’re out.

steps.prompt: 4% of $750,000 is how many dollars in year one?
Roth IRA owners must take required minimums at 73.
steps.explain: Not during the owner’s lifetime. Traditional IRAs are the age-73 account.

steps.prompt: A $200,000 pile falls 20% and you then withdraw $10,000. How many dollars are left?
In the common draw order, which account waits until last?
steps.explain: Roth last. Taxable first, traditional in the middle.
